body_markdown:
Cluster API (CAPI) is really quite a beautiful thing: it brings declarative, Kubernetes® style APIs to cluster lifecycle management, turning infrastructure provisioning from a tangle of brittle scripts into standard reconciliation loops.


However, anyone who has managed Kubernetes clusters with Cluster API in production environments may encounter that creating a raw Cluster resource is only half the battle. A raw cluster isn’t even ready until you’ve installed a CNI, and it’s certainly not production-ready until you’ve configured container registry mirrors, HTTP proxies, audit policies, cloud provider integrations, and CSI drivers.


In this post, we’ll look at how Cluster API’s ClusterClass and Runtime SDK fit together, why complex ClusterClass definitions can quickly become unwieldy, and how we built **Cluster API Runtime Extensions – Nutanix (CAREN)** to provide a single, strongly typed Cluster resource experience for describing a Kubernetes cluster with selected foundational components configured.


## The Evolution of Cluster API Topologies


When Cluster API first started out (many moons ago), provisioning a cluster meant applying a sprawling bundle of YAML manifests: a` Cluster` , an infrastructure cluster (like` NutanixCluster` ,` AWSCluster` , or` DockerCluster` ), a` KubeadmControlPlane` , plus` MachineDeployment` ,` KubeadmConfigTemplate` , and infrastructure machine template resources for every worker pool.


To solve this boilerplate explosion, Cluster API introduced` ClusterClass` and managed topologies. With ClusterClass, platform engineers define a reusable template for a cluster’s shape once, and users stamp out clusters from a single, concise` Cluster` manifest using` spec.topology` .


Here’s where it gets interesting. To make a` ClusterClass` reusable across different environments, you need to expose configuration knobs via cluster variables and apply them to the underlying templates using inline JSON patches.


- For one or two simple settings—say, changing an instance type or a Kubernetes image repository—inline JSON patches in a` ClusterClass` work great.
- When you need to configure 30+ day-1 and day-2 settings across multiple providers (proxy settings with systemd drop-ins, custom NTP servers, etcd encryption at rest, containerd registry mirrors with TLS certificates, and conditional addon installations), inline YAML patching becomes tedious and error-prone.
- Testing complex Go templates and JSON6902 patches embedded inside hundreds of lines of YAML is nobody’s idea of fun. Who wants to debug whitespace issues in nested YAML strings when you have a full programming language available?


## Enter Cluster API Runtime Extensions (and CAREN)


Thankfully, the Cluster API maintainers foresaw this exact problem and introduced the **Runtime SDK** —a mechanism that allows external components to hook directly into the Cluster API topology controller and cluster lifecycle via strongly-typed HTTP webhooks.


That brings us to **[Cluster API Runtime Extensions – Nutanix (CAREN)](https://github.com/nutanix-cloud-native/cluster-api-runtime-extensions-nutanix/)** . Despite having Nutanix in the repo name, CAREN isn’t just for Nutanix infrastructure—it supports Nutanix, AWS, and Docker (CAPD) out of the box, alongside a large suite of generic Kubernetes and kubeadm customizations.


The goal of CAREN is simple: **the Cluster resource should be the single place a user interacts with to describe a fully operational Kubernetes cluster.**


Instead of maintaining fragile inline patches in your` ClusterClass` , CAREN acts as a Cluster API Runtime Extension that does two heavy-lifting jobs in Go code:


1. **Topology Mutation (DiscoverVariables, GeneratePatches, ValidateTopology):** During topology reconciliation, CAREN injects rich, OpenAPI-validated schema variables (` clusterConfig` and` workerConfig` ) into your` ClusterClass` and dynamically mutates the underlying` KubeadmControlPlane` ,` KubeadmConfigTemplate` , and infrastructure machine templates.
2. **Lifecycle Hooks (AfterControlPlaneInitialized, BeforeClusterDelete, etc.):** Once the control plane comes up, CAREN hooks into the cluster lifecycle to automatically install and configure essential cluster addons—such as your CNI (Cilium or Calico), CSI storage drivers, Cloud Controller Managers (CCM), Node Feature Discovery (NFD), and service load balancers—using either` ClusterResourceSets` (CRS) or the Cluster API Addon Provider for Helm (CAAPH).


## What Does CAREN Manage?


Because CAREN’s mutation and lifecycle handlers are written in Go, we can compose clean, modular handlers that are thoroughly unit- and e2e-tested. We’ve split these capabilities into three main areas:


- **Generic & Kubeadm Customizations:** Configure global image registry mirrors, HTTP/HTTPS proxies, custom image registries with credentials/CA certs, NTP servers, node taints, SSH users, audit policies, etcd flags, encryption at rest, kube-proxy modes, and Pod Security Admission—all from simple fields on the` Cluster` resource.
- **Infrastructure-Specific Customizations:**


- **Nutanix:** Prism Central endpoints, control plane endpoints (including kube-vip integration), and machine sizing/categories.
- **AWS:** AMI specs, placement groups, security groups, IAM instance profiles, and control plane load balancers.
- **Docker:** Custom kindest/node images for fast local testing.


- **Cluster Addons & Lifecycle Handlers:** Turnkey deployment of CNI (Cilium, Calico), CSI (Nutanix CSI, AWS EBS, local-path), CCM, Cluster Autoscaler, COSI, Node Feature Discovery, and automatic garbage collection of LoadBalancer Services before cluster deletion so cloud teardowns don’t hang on orphaned load balancers.


## Let’s Try It Out!


Let’s work through a hands-on example using a local KinD management cluster and the Cluster API Docker provider (CAPD). Skip straight ahead to inspecting the Cluster manifest if you’re already familiar with setting up CAPI locally—we’re going to spin up a management cluster with CAREN installed and deploy a Docker workload cluster with Cilium CNI automatically configured via Helm.


### 1. Spin Up a Local Management Cluster


If you have the CAREN repository cloned (and if you read my previous post on Devbox, you’ll be pleased to know the repo includes a devbox.json so you don’t have to install kind, clusterctl, or helm manually!), you can bootstrap a local KinD cluster with all required providers and CAREN deployed via a single Make target:


```text
make dev.run-on-kind
eval $(make kind.kubeconfig)
```


If you’re installing CAREN onto an existing Cluster API management cluster, you can install it directly via clusterctl or Helm (just make sure` EXP_TOPOLOGY=true` and` EXP_RUNTIME_SDK=true` are enabled on your CAPI controllers).


### 2. How ClusterClass Hooks Into CAREN


Let’s look at how clean a ClusterClass becomes when CAREN handles the mutations. Instead of hundreds of lines of inline variable definitions and JSON patches, your ClusterClass simply references CAREN’s external patch and lifecycle extensions:


```text
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterClass
metadata:
name: docker-quick-start
spec:
# ... controlPlane, infrastructure, and workers templates ...
patches:
- name: cluster-config
external:
generateExtension: dockerclusterconfigpatch-generate.caren.nutanix.com
validateExtension: dockerclusterconfigpatch-validate.caren.nutanix.com
discoverVariablesExtension: dockerclusterconfigvars-discover.caren.nutanix.com
```


When you apply this` ClusterClass` , CAPI calls CAREN’s` discoverVariablesExtension` webhook. CAREN responds with the complete OpenAPI schema for` clusterConfig` and` workerConfig` tailored to that infrastructure provider. You get full server-side schema validation on your` Cluster` variables without writing a single line of OpenAPI schema by hand!


### 3. Create a Workload Cluster with Cilium and Custom Settings


Now let’s look at what the user actually interacts with: the` Cluster` resource. Notice how we configure our CNI addon (Cilium via the Helm addon provider) and custom Kubernetes settings right inside the` clusterConfig` variable:


```text
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
name: docker-cluster-cilium
spec:
topology:
class: docker-quick-start
version: v1.35.3
controlPlane:
replicas: 1
workers:
machineDeployments:
- class: default-worker
name: md-0
replicas: 1
variables:
- name: clusterConfig
value:
addons:
cni:
provider: Cilium
strategy: HelmAddon
users:
- name: devops
sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
```


Let’s generate and apply one of the example clusters from the repository using` clusterctl` and Server-Side Apply:


```text
export CLUSTER_NAME=docker-cluster-cilium-helm-addon
export CLUSTER_FILE=examples/capi-quick-start/docker-cluster-cilium-helm-addon.yaml
export KUBERNETES_VERSION=v1.35.3


clusterctl generate cluster ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
--from ${CLUSTER_FILE} \
--kubernetes-version ${KUBERNETES_VERSION} \
--worker-machine-count 1 | \
kubectl apply --server-side -f -
```


Wait for the control plane to initialize:


```text
kubectl wait clusters/${CLUSTER_NAME} --for=condition=ControlPlaneInitialized --timeout=5m
```


Behind the scenes, two things just happened:


1. Before the machines were created, CAREN’s topology mutation hooks patched the` KubeadmControlPlane` and` KubeadmConfigTemplate` with all the required containerd, kubelet, and control plane configurations.
2. The moment` ControlPlaneInitialized` flipped to` True` , CAPI triggered CAREN’s` AfterControlPlaneInitialized` lifecycle hook, which instructed the Helm addon provider to install Cilium onto the new workload cluster.


Let’s grab the workload cluster’s kubeconfig and verify that our nodes are ready and Cilium is up and running:


```text
clusterctl get kubeconfig ${CLUSTER_NAME} > ${CLUSTER_NAME}.conf


# Wait for nodes to become Ready (proving CNI is healthy)
kubectl --kubeconfig ${CLUSTER_NAME}.conf wait nodes --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=5m


# Inspect the Cilium DaemonSet
kubectl --kubeconfig ${CLUSTER_NAME}.conf get daemonsets -n kube-system cilium


NAME     DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR            AGE
cilium   2         2         2       2            2           kubernetes.io/os=linux   2m14s
```


Perfect! With a single Cluster resource, we went from zero to a ready workload cluster with our chosen CNI and node customizations applied automatically.


## Wrapping Up


Cluster API’s ClusterClass and Runtime SDK are a massive leap forward for declarative Kubernetes lifecycle management. By moving complex topology mutations and addon lifecycle orchestration out of inline YAML patches and into modular, tested Go handlers, **CAREN** gives platform teams the best of both worlds: a clean, maintainable codebase for cluster extensions, and a simple, self-service Cluster API for end users.


Check out the[CAREN documentation](https://nutanix-cloud-native.github.io/cluster-api-runtime-extensions-nutanix/) and the[GitHub repository](https://github.com/nutanix-cloud-native/cluster-api-runtime-extensions-nutanix/) to explore all the supported customizations, addons, and example ClusterClass definitions. Contributions, issues, and feedback are always welcome!
